source_title: Chain-of-Defensive-Thought: Structured Reasoning Elicits Robustness in Large Language Models against Reference Corruption
baselines_compared: Standard prompting (no defensive reasoning) as the primary baseline, evaluated identically across the same 18 models, 2 benchmarks, and 2 attack types; no comparison against other RAG-defense methods (e.g., certified-robust RAG) is reported in the excerpted sections
key_result: On Natural Questions, GPT-4o's accuracy collapses from 60% to 3% under reference corruption with standard prompting, but chain-of-defensive-thought (CoDT) restores it to 50%; across the full 18-model, 2-benchmark, 2-attack-type evaluation, CoDT gives an average accuracy increase of 23.70% and an average attack-success-rate decrease of 27.31%, with no loss of clean-setting accuracy, and improves Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct's minimum accuracy under corruption by 35 points (16%->51%).
technical_summary: Proposes chain-of-defensive-thought (CoDT), a pure few-shot prompting technique that has the LLM first identify which of its provided references are relevant and which are reliable, and articulate this as an explicit reasoning step, before answering - mimicking a human cross-checking multiple sources. Requires no training, no additional dataset, and works identically on open models and black-box APIs. Evaluates across 18 LLMs on Natural Questions and RealTime QA against two reference-corruption attack types (prompt injection and PoisonedRAG-style knowledge corruption), showing large, consistent robustness gains with no loss of clean accuracy.
datasets_benchmarks: Natural Questions and RealTime QA, using the top-10 retrieved passages per query collected by Xiang et al. (2024); first 100 samples per dataset, with the last of 10 references corrupted under each attack

source_title: Prompt Injection Vulnerability of Consensus Generating Applications in Digital Democracy
baselines_compared: No-defense (ND) condition compared against defense-layer ablations: GPT-OSSafeGuard + structured representations alone (G+S) versus the full pipeline with GSPO fine-tuning added (G+S+GSPO); also compared against DPO+GSPO and a deliberative-alignment (DA) methodology as alternative alignment approaches
key_result: Default LLaMA 3.1 8B, GPT-4.1 Nano, and Apertus 8B show widespread vulnerability to prompt injection especially when public opinion is finely balanced, with attacks shifting consensus toward GB-unionist conservative framing over pro-independence framing and rational/instruction-like rhetorical strategies proving most effective; the authors' robustness pipeline (GPT-OSS-SafeGuard detection + structured opinion representations + GSPO-based reinforcement learning) substantially reduces directional failures whenever the true consensus has a clear positive or negative valence, though ambiguous near-neutral cases remain difficult even with the defense.
technical_summary: Examines the vulnerability of off-the-shelf LLMs used to generate consensus statements in digital-democracy applications to prompt-injection attacks that amplify, erase, or redirect opinions. Constructs attack-free and adversarial prompt variants over public-policy questions, classifies opinion/consensus valence with a fine-tuned BERT model, and measures LLM-human majority agreement rates across three LLMs. Finds vulnerabilities concentrated in politically balanced deliberations and favoring certain rhetorical/political framings. Proposes a robustness pipeline combining an existing injection detector (GPT-OSS-SafeGuard), structured opinion representations, and GSPO-based reinforcement learning fine-tuning, evaluated with layer-wise ablations, showing substantial but incomplete recovery of directional accuracy.
datasets_benchmarks: Tessler et al. (2024) collective-statements dataset (462 prompts), expanded to 6,020 unique adversarial/attack-free prompt variants (80 human-readable injection alternatives x 2x2x20 variation grid); a fine-tuned BERT model used to classify opinion/consensus valence for evaluation

source_title: Data Defenses Against Large Language Models
baselines_compared: Prior mitigations - text anonymization and model alignment/safety training - shown to be largely ineffective against LLM inference/privacy attacks, contrasted with the paper's own data defenses across multiple attacker LLMs, datasets, and defeat-attempting countermeasures
key_result: On the news RAG benchmark, applying the defense to each retrieved article individually reduces gpt-4o-2024-05-13 answer accuracy from 80% to under 20% across many countermeasures (no countermeasure restores accuracy above 50%), and reduces meta-llama-3.1-8B-instruct accuracy from 35% to 0%; on synthetic Reddit/Wikipedia PII-inference tasks the defenses prevent attacker success roughly 75% of the time, versus prior anonymization and model-alignment mitigations which the authors show are largely ineffective against these attacks.
technical_summary: Introduces 'data defenses,' a novel privacy-protection strategy that flips the typical adversarial-ML framing: instead of protecting LLM deployers from malicious users, it empowers data owners (writers, journalists, social-media users) against LLMs used to infer their PII or misappropriate their content. Automatically generates short adversarial prompt-injection-style text strings that, when inserted into a document, significantly reduce an LLM's ability to accurately infer personal attributes or answer questions about that content, while remaining minimally invasive to human readers. Evaluates across synthetic Reddit profiles, Wikipedia biographies, and a real-world news RAG benchmark, against multiple attacker LLMs and countermeasures attempting to strip the defense, achieving over 90% effectiveness on many datasets.
datasets_benchmarks: Synthetic Reddit-profile dataset (n=75) for benchmarking privacy-attack defenses; Wikipedia biographies dataset (n=75); a news RAG benchmark (Retrieval Augmented Generation Benchmark) with five real news articles per query scraped from CNN, AP, and other publishers

source_title: DP-Fusion: Token-Level Differentially Private Inference for Large Language Models
baselines_compared: DP-Prompt and DP-Decoding (prior differentially-private-inference baselines) and simple NER/prompt-engineering empirical baselines, compared on the privacy/utility (perplexity) trade-off for document privatization and on attack success rate for the RAG-poisoning jailbreak experiment
key_result: DP-Fusion achieves roughly 6x lower perplexity (higher utility) than the strongest baseline differentially-private-inference method (DP-Prompt) at comparable privacy levels (1.426 vs. baseline PPL range), and in a dedicated RAG-based prompt-injection jailbreak experiment (HotPotQA, single poisoned chunk achieving >=90% ASR undefended), DP-Fusion reduces attack success rate to 0% at appropriate privacy-budget settings, while baseline DPI methods (DP-Decoding, DP-Prompt) leave much higher residual ASR.
technical_summary: Proposes DP-Fusion, a Differentially Private Inference (DPI) mechanism that provably bounds how much a labeled subset of context tokens can influence an LLM's output distribution, by computing a baseline distribution without sensitive tokens, a distribution with them, and blending the two within a bounded divergence controlled by a privacy parameter epsilon. Applies this primarily to document privatization - paraphrasing text containing PII so it cannot be reliably inferred while preserving text quality - achieving substantially better privacy/utility trade-offs than prior DPI baselines. Additionally demonstrates, in a dedicated experiment, that the same per-token influence bound serves as a defense against RAG-based prompt-injection jailbreaks, reducing attack success rate to 0% in a HotPotQA poisoned-retrieval setting where undefended models are jailbroken at >=90% ASR.
datasets_benchmarks: Document-privatization evaluation datasets (PII-bearing documents; specific corpus not named in excerpted text); a RAG-poisoning jailbreak evaluation built on HotPotQA with a single poisoned retrieval chunk

source_title: Zero-Shot Embedding Drift Detection: A Lightweight Defense Against Prompt Injections in LLMs
baselines_compared: Prior embedding-based classification approaches (Logistic Regression, XGBoost, Random Forest on embeddings) from a cited comparison study; positioned against heavier detection approaches relying on additional large models or rule-based filters
key_result: ZEDD detects direct and indirect prompt injections with greater than 93% accuracy across Llama 3, Qwen 2, and Mistral embedding spaces, with a false positive rate below 3%, outperforming prior embedding-drift approaches that rely on Logistic Regression/XGBoost/Random Forest classifiers on top of embeddings rather than the drift signal itself, per the paper's comparison figure against a cited prior study.
technical_summary: Introduces Zero-Shot Embedding Drift Detection (ZEDD), a lightweight, model-agnostic defense that detects both direct and indirect prompt injection by measuring cosine-similarity drift between the embeddings of a candidate input and its cleaned/benign counterpart, requiring no model internals access, no prior attack-type knowledge, and no task-specific retraining. Re-annotates the LLMail-Inject dataset across five injection categories to build adversarial-clean prompt pairs for evaluation, achieving greater than 93% detection accuracy with under 3% false positives across three open LLM embedding spaces, and provides qualitative case analyses of how the cleaning process neutralizes specific injection categories (jailbreak, system-leak, task-override, encoding-manipulation attacks).
datasets_benchmarks: Re-annotated Microsoft LLMail-Inject dataset (adversarial emails targeting LLM-integrated assistants via indirect prompt injection), spanning five injection categories, split roughly 70/30 train/test

source_title: PhantomLint: Principled Detection of Hidden LLM Prompts in Structured Documents
baselines_compared: None - no competing detector is run head-to-head; the paper argues analytically that text-only prompt-injection detectors cannot distinguish visible from hidden instructions and so must produce false alarms, and it reimplements Xiong et al.'s malicious-font hiding method as an attack to defeat rather than as a defense baseline.
key_result: PhantomLint detected the hidden prompt in all 26 synthetic documents across every hiding method tested (white text, invisible OCG ViewState /OFF, text render mode 3, off-CropBox and off-MediaBox placement, malicious blank-glyph fonts, HTML hidden visibility), and in all 113 real hidden-prompt documents, with no alarms on the 6 visible-prompt negatives. On 3,257 ICML 2025 papers it raised only 3 alarms, all OCR-failure false positives, giving a false-positive rate of approximately 0.092%. Mean runtime was 68.25 s per ICML paper and 43.75 s per real-world document.
technical_summary: Proposes the first hiding-method-agnostic detector for hidden LLM prompts in structured documents, framed as a metamorphic test. Applies an ANALYZE step that flags text spans resembling LLM instructions, then an OCR consistency test that renders the minimal document region containing the suspicious block, OCRs it, and treats text present in extraction but absent from OCR as evidence of hiding; a detection requires the intersection of suspicious and hidden spans to be non-empty. Implements this in the PhantomLint prototype for PDF and HTML. Evaluates generality on 26 synthetic documents covering seven hiding techniques, false-positive rate on 3,257 ICML 2025 papers, practical utility on 119 curated real documents, and runtime.
datasets_benchmarks: 26 author-built synthetic documents (16 PDF, 10 HTML) spanning the known text-hiding methods; all 3,257 accepted ICML 2025 papers from OpenReview (false-positive corpus); 119 curated real-world documents containing LLM prompts (113 hidden/positive, 6 visible/negative; 93 PDF, 26 HTML; CVs, arXiv preprints, theses, a book chapter, blogs, one email). 3,402 documents total.

source_title: CAPTURE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Testing and Robustness Enhancement
baselines_compared: Five off-the-shelf prompt guardrail models (PromptGuard, Deepset, Fmops, ProtectAI v2, InjecGuard) and two LLM-based detectors (GPT-4o, Llama3.2-1B-Instruct). Note that baseline numbers on the external NotInject/WildGuard/BIPIA benchmarks are taken from the InjecGuard paper rather than re-run by the authors.
key_result: Existing guardrails fail badly on context-aware attacks framed in an application's own domain: Fmops reaches 100% false negative rate while PromptGuard reaches 100% false positive rate, and InjecGuard and ProtectAI v2 show high FNR and FPR simultaneously. CaptureGuard, trained on CAPTURE-generated data, achieves near-zero FNR (0.00-0.15%) and FPR (0.00-2.05%) on the tested domains, and generalizes externally with 79.04% on NotInject (vs InjecGuard 87.32%), 75.00% on WildGuard (vs InjecGuard 76.11%) and 54.77% on BIPIA Injection, well above ProtectAI v2.
technical_summary: Introduces CAPTURE, a generation framework and benchmark for testing prompt-injection guardrails under application-specific context rather than static attack lists. Builds attacks from the Framework/Separator/Disruptor decomposition of Liu et al., systematically varying each component with GPT-4o over six application domains, and pairs MALICIOUS-GEN adversarial prompts with SAFE-GEN benign prompts that contain trigger words in order to measure over-defense alongside detection. Evaluates five production guardrail models plus two LLM detectors, exposing simultaneous false-negative and false-positive failure modes. Then fine-tunes three domain-specific DeBERTaV3-base classifiers, CaptureGuard, on the generated data using InjecGuard's training recipe, and shows near-zero FNR and FPR in-domain with competitive transfer to NotInject, WildGuard and BIPIA.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces the CAPTURE benchmark: MALICIOUS-GEN (context-aware attacks) and SAFE-GEN (benign over-defense probes) generated with GPT-4o across six application domains (Shopping, Covid, Movies, Stock, Travel, Python Code), seeded from public QA datasets with 30 train / 15 test / 15 validation base questions per domain expanded to 100 examples per domain per split. External benchmarks for generalization: NotInject, WildGuard, BIPIA (Injection).

baselines_compared: No-defense baseline, perplexity filtering (Jain et al. 2023), and RA-LLM (Cao et al. 2023)
key_result: SPIN reduces attack success rate by up to 87.9% overall, driving ASR to 12.11% (Vicuna) and 0% (Llama-2) against GCG universal-trigger attacks and to 0% against natural-language jailbreak/role-play attacks on both models, while preserving benign TriviaQA performance; against an adaptive attacker aware of the defense, ASR is still cut by up to 76%.
technical_summary: Proposes SPIN (Self-Supervised Prompt INjection), a training-free, inference-time defense against jailbreak and adversarial-suffix attacks. Introduces two self-supervised detection tasks - a 'repeat' task scored by Levenshtein distance and an 'interjection' task testing whether the model can still answer a known factual question - to flag malicious inputs, plus a 'reversal' layer that prepends and optimizes tokens to minimize input perplexity and restore refusal behavior for inputs that slip through detection. Evaluates on Llama-2 and Vicuna against GCG universal adversarial triggers, handcrafted jailbreaks, adversarial instructions, role-play/DAN attacks and automated jailbreak generators (AutoDAN, CodeChameleon, ICA), reducing attack success rate by up to 87.9% while preserving benign TriviaQA accuracy. Also analyzes an adaptive attacker who jointly optimizes against the attack objective and the self-supervised defense signals, showing the defense still cuts ASR by up to 76%.
datasets_benchmarks: AdvBench 'harmful behaviors' (520 prompts) with GCG-optimized universal adversarial-trigger suffixes; TriviaQA (benign utility check); Jailbreak Chat top-5 upvoted prompts paired with 150 AdvBench requests; Wei et al. 2023 adversarial-instruction attack paired with 150 requests; role-play/'dev mode v2' DAN-style attack paired with 150 requests; automated jailbreak generators AutoDAN, CodeChameleon, ICA each paired with 150 requests

source_title: Quantifying Conversation Drift in MCP via Latent Polytope
baselines_compared: Sandwich Prevention, Instructional Prevention, and Known-Answer Detection (all from Liu et al. 2024's prompt-injection benchmarking framework)
key_result: SecMCP achieves AUROC above 0.915 in every scenario (average ~0.98, exceeding 0.99 in several hijacking cases) across 3 LLMs x 3 datasets x 3 risk types, and clearly outperforms Sandwich Prevention, Instructional Prevention, and Known-Answer Detection baselines; under an adaptive synonym-replacement attack, AUROC drops by roughly 0.12-0.13 but the method still detects most attacks.
technical_summary: Proposes SecMCP, a detection framework that quantifies 'conversation drift' in Model Context Protocol (MCP)-powered agent systems by modeling LLM activation vectors within a latent polytope space. Computes layer-wise activation-vector deviation between an incoming query and a bank of anchor points drawn from legitimate queries, then uses a distance-based decision-tree classifier (Risk Matching) to flag inputs whose deviation from the authorized region exceeds a threshold. Evaluates on three open-source LLMs (Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, Vicuna-7B) against tool-poisoning and indirect-prompt-injection attacks realizing three risks - hijacking, misleading, and data exfiltration - across FinQA, HotpotQA and MS MARCO, achieving AUROC consistently above 0.915 and outperforming three prior defense baselines, with a robustness check against synonym-replacement adaptive attacks.
datasets_benchmarks: FinQA, HotpotQA, MS MARCO (used to build MCP-server resource pools and query sets); 1,000 ChatGPT-4.5-generated data-exfiltration prompts across 10 attack categories (100 each); PoisonedRAG-style misleading documents seeded with a synthetic fake-news corpus; HijackRAG-style hijacking segments embedded in retrieved documents

source_title: CASCADE: A Cascaded Hybrid Defense Architecture for Prompt Injection Detection in MCP-Based Systems
baselines_compared: None - no external MCP defense system was reimplemented or run on this corpus; the paper explicitly states literature figures for other MCP defenses are quoted descriptively (Table 1) under different datasets/protocols and support no comparative claim. The 'comparison' performed is an internal ablation across the paper's own three configurations (rule-only, rule+semantic, rule+semantic+LLM review).
key_result: Component ablation on the frozen corpus: rule-based layer alone reaches 61.05% recall (95% CI 59.42-62.66), adding the BGE semantic stage raises recall to 94.77% (93.98-95.46); counting human-review referrals as positives reports an 11.70% false-positive rate versus 1.51% if only outright denials count (a 7.7x difference), and 68.5% of traffic reaches a human reviewer under that convention; recall is not provenance-invariant, ranging from 86.20% on original material to 99.88% on template-generated material; the optional local Llama3 review stage is invoked on 32.56% of requests at 2.51s each but changes zero final classifications.
technical_summary: Introduces CASCADE (Cascaded Analysis for Secure Content And Detection Engine), a fully local three-layer defense for MCP-based systems combining regex/entropy pre-filtering, BGE-embedding semantic analysis with an optional local-Llama3 ambiguous-case review, and a pattern-based output filter, exposing a three-valued ALLOW/REVIEW/BLOCK decision interface. The paper's larger contribution, however, is a methodological audit of how MCP-defense evaluations are reported: it shows the choice of aggregation convention (counting human-review referrals as false positives versus only outright denials) changes the headline false-positive rate by a factor of 7.7, that detection recall is highly provenance-dependent (86.20% on original vs 99.88% on template-generated material), that the true operating threshold used in the released system cannot be read off the published configuration and must be recovered from the score distribution, and that the optional LLM review stage, while invoked on a third of traffic, changes no final classification outcome. All findings come from a fully reproducible, digest-pinned 5,000-sample corpus with per-sample released decision records.
datasets_benchmarks: A frozen, self-assembled 5,000-sample MCP-attack corpus drawn from multiple third-party collections (e.g., VulnerableMCP entries, GitHub adversarial commands, a prompt-injection dataset) plus template-generated/synthetic material; audited in full for provenance class, exact-duplicate rate (27.0% repeated text) and reference-set overlap

source_title: SecureCAI: Injection-Resilient LLM Assistants for Cybersecurity Operations
baselines_compared: Base LLM (no safety training), Standard Constitutional AI (Bai et al.), Input Filtering (perplexity-based adversarial detection), and Instruction Hierarchy (priority-based prompt processing)
key_result: SecureCAI reduces average attack success rate to 4.3%, versus 80.4% for the base LLM (94.7% reduction) and 40.4% for standard Constitutional AI (89.4% reduction); maintains Constitutional Adherence Score above 0.92 under increasing adversarial pressure (vs. standard CAI dropping from 0.92 to 0.48); improves rather than degrades clean-task accuracy relative to baselines; and generalizes to held-out attack categories at 7.9% ASR versus 50.5% for standard CAI, at a cost of roughly 23% higher inference latency.
technical_summary: Introduces SecureCAI, a defense framework that extends Constitutional AI with security-aware constitutional principles, adaptive constitution evolution driven by continuous red-teaming, and a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) stage for unlearning unsafe attack-compliant response patterns, targeting prompt injection attacks embedded in cybersecurity artifacts (logs, phishing emails, malware samples). Trains an unspecified 7B-parameter base model through a four-stage pipeline (constitutional supervised fine-tuning, security-adapted DPO, unsafe-pattern unlearning, deployment with red-teaming feedback) and evaluates against base-LLM, standard-CAI, input-filtering, and instruction-hierarchy baselines on a self-constructed adversarial dataset. Reports large reductions in attack success rate, improved robustness under sustained adversarial pressure, generalization to unseen attack categories, and ablations isolating the contribution of each framework component, at a moderate inference-latency cost.
datasets_benchmarks: A self-constructed adversarial dataset of 51,750 adversarial samples spanning log poisoning, phishing/email content, and malware-code injection attack vectors, built from unspecified 'operational environments and public threat intelligence sources'; not released or otherwise publicly identified

defense_name: LLM-as-a-Judge (taxonomy-guided structured-reasoning judge) with Mixture-of-Models aggregation
source_title: Prompt Attack Detection with LLM-as-a-Judge and Mixture-of-Models
baselines_compared: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, OpenAI Guardrails, encoder-based prompt-injection classifiers, and specialized fine-tuned safety/security LLMs
key_result: The best single LLM-judge (gpt-5.1) achieves F1=0.8711 (precision 0.9766), exceeding the best specialized fine-tuned safety/security model (F1=0.8041) and encoder-based classifiers (very low F1); even the fastest judge (gemini-2.5/2.0-flash-lite) surpasses the best specialized security model; Mixture-of-Models ensembling gives only modest, inconsistent gains (best triple mixture gpt-5.1+gpt-5-mini+claude-haiku-4.5 reaches F1=0.9014, some pairwise/triple mixtures instead degrade performance by up to ~3%); the gemini-2.0-flash-lite-001 configuration is deployed in production as a centralized guardrail for Singapore public-service chatbots.
technical_summary: Proposes an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for real-time prompt-attack detection that replaces opaque binary yes/no prompting with a structured, taxonomy-guided reasoning process: framing-stripping, categorization into workflow instruction/factual overview/safety knowledge/detailed harm methods/safety-bypass-attempt, multi-turn context analysis, and mandatory self-reflection before a final verdict and confidence score. Also introduces a parallel Mixture-of-Models (MoM) architecture that combines multiple LLM judges via a weighted linear score aggregation optimized for F1. Evaluates on a private curated dataset of real production chatbot traffic plus automated red-teaming attacks, showing lightweight general-purpose LLM judges outperform encoder-based classifiers, specialized fine-tuned safety models, and commercial guardrail products (Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, OpenAI Guardrails), while MoM ensembling yields only modest and inconsistent additional gains. The gemini-2.0-flash-lite-001 single-judge configuration is deployed in production as a centralized guardrail service for Singapore public-sector chatbots.
datasets_benchmarks: A private curated evaluation dataset of 929 prompts (770 benign, 82.9%; 159 adversarial, 17.1%) combining real-world public-sector chatbot queries with adversarial prompts generated via automated red teaming (ART); evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation for the Mixture-of-Models experiments

source_title: Know Thy Enemy: Securing LLMs Against Prompt Injection via Diverse Data Synthesis and Instruction-Level Chain-of-Thought Learning
baselines_compared: External-detector defenses and post-training/model-enhancement defenses including MetaSec and other prior instruction-alignment approaches (Chen et al. 2025b/c/d, Wu et al. 2025), plus the four existing PI-defense datasets compared for diversity
key_result: Averaged across four LLMs, InstruCoT reaches Defense Rates of 92.5% (Behavior Deviation), 98.0% (Privacy Leakage), and 90.9% (Harmful Output), outperforming baselines by 25.8-82.5 points in Behavior Deviation, 6.7-47.2 points in Privacy Leakage, and 7.4-34.5 points in Harmful Output, with no utility degradation versus baseline methods; for Behavior Deviation specifically it reaches 91.5% DR on direct injection and 93.4% on indirect injection.
technical_summary: Proposes InstruCoT, an instruction-level safety-alignment method that defends LLMs against prompt injection by (1) synthesizing a diverse training dataset spanning three threat scenarios (behavior deviation, privacy leakage, harmful output), multiple context-region injection positions, and (2) fine-tuning the LLM on chain-of-thought reasoning traces - inspired by Endsley's Situation Awareness model - that guide it to perceive all instructions in context, judge whether each violates the system prompt's scope, and decide which to follow or refuse. Evaluates on four open-source LLMs (Llama3.1-8B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B), showing large Defense Rate gains over external-detector and prior post-training defense baselines across all three threat dimensions with no loss in benign-task utility, and releases both dataset and code.
datasets_benchmarks: Synthetic instruction-level CoT training dataset built from three clean-prompt sources (Alpaca-clean, SystemChat, and a third dataset) with GPT-4.1-generated adversarial injections spanning multiple context regions and three threat dimensions (Behavior Deviation, Privacy Leakage, Harmful Output); compared against four existing PI-defense datasets on injection/scenario diversity via manual review; evaluation test sets share threat dimensions with training but contain non-overlapping instructions

source_title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
baselines_compared: Full recomputation (quality reference, high cost), delete-and-shift (with RoPE re-rotation), instruction-only forgetting (prompt-based selective forgetting per LLM memory-benchmark literature), and local suffix repair (partial suffix recomputation)
key_result: On the controlled NIAH-style benchmark, KVEraser nearly matches full recomputation's post-erasure quality across 1K-32K context lengths while its latency increases only 24% versus a 17.6x latency increase for full recomputation; on unseen long-document QA with harmful distractors, KVEraser achieves the highest exact match among approximate baselines with a 3-4x speedup over full recomputation, landing on the quality-efficiency Pareto frontier where the strongest baseline (local suffix repair) trails in quality.
technical_summary: Introduces KVEraser, a learned KV-cache editing method that performs efficient, localized 'context erasing': given a processed context and a span to remove (e.g., a stale retrieved fact, an incorrect tool observation, a retracted user preference, or a harmful injected instruction), it replaces only that span's cached KV states with learned steering states while reusing the rest of the cache unchanged, avoiding the suffix-length-dependent cost of full recomputation. Trains a two-stage pipeline (generic span-neighbor pre-training, then task-specific fine-tuning) on Qwen3-8B and evaluates against full recomputation and three approximate baselines (delete-and-shift, instruction-only forgetting, local suffix repair) on a controlled synthetic erasing benchmark (1K-32K context) and on unseen long-document QA with harmful factual distractors, achieving near-full-recomputation quality at a fraction of the latency cost and the best quality-efficiency tradeoff among approximate methods.
datasets_benchmarks: A controlled synthetic 'Erasing needle in a haystack' (NIAH) benchmark isolating post-hoc span deletion across 1K-32K context lengths, built from Natural Questions/HotpotQA/TriviaQA-style passages; and long-document QA with harmful factual distractors mined from non-gold Wikipedia pages, trained on one QA source and evaluated zero-shot on three unseen datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, IIRC)
